# The model

We model the recovery of visual sensitivity during dark adaptation with the function
$$
\text{thres}(t) = ct + cc\,e^{-t/\tau} + S2\,(t-\alpha)\,H(t-\alpha),
$$
where:

- $\text{thres}(t)$ is the measured threshold at time $t$ after bleach;
- $ct$ is the cone threshold, the plateau to which cone-mediated sensitivity recovers;
- $cc$ is the cone coefficient, the amplitude of the cone recovery component;
- $\tau$ is the cone time constant;
- $S2$ is the slope of the second (rod-mediated) component of recovery;
- $\alpha$ is the rod-cone break, the time at which rod recovery begins;
- $H(t-\alpha)$ is the Heaviside step function, equal to $0$ for $t < \alpha$ and $1$ for $t \geq \alpha$.

The term $(t-\alpha)H(t-\alpha)$ is therefore a ramp: it is zero before the rod-cone break and changes linearly with slope $S2$ after it.

## Rewriting the model in a familiar form

Most STEM scientists are familiar with the equation of a straight line,
$$
y = c + mx,
$$
where $y$ is the response, $x$ is the independent variable, $c$ is the intercept and $m$ is the gradient. Fitting this line to data by ordinary least squares (OLS) has a closed-form solution: no iteration, no starting guesses.

Our aim is to show that, under one condition, our model has exactly the same character. We want to reach the form
$$
\mathbf{Y} = a + \mathbf{B}\,\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}),
$$
where $\mathbf{Y}$ is the vector of participant responses, $\mathbf{x}$ is the vector of response time stamps, $a$ is an intercept, $\mathbf{F}$ is a set of basis functions evaluated at those time stamps, and $\mathbf{B}$ is a vector of coefficients. This is the straight-line equation with the single term $mx$ replaced by a sum of curved terms.

Suppose the two nonlinear parameters, $\tau$ and $\alpha$, are held fixed. Then define two basis functions:
$$
f_1(\mathbf{x}) = e^{-\mathbf{x}/\tau}, \qquad
f_2(\mathbf{x}) = (\mathbf{x}-\alpha)\,H(\mathbf{x}-\alpha).
$$
The model becomes
$$
\mathbf{Y} = ct + cc\,f_1(\mathbf{x}) + S2\,f_2(\mathbf{x}) = a + \mathbf{B}\,\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}),
$$
with $a = ct$ playing the role of the intercept $c$, and $\mathbf{B} = (cc,\ S2)$. This is a linear model. Every quantity we do not know appears only as an intercept or a multiplying coefficient. Those familiar with OLS will recognise that the best-fitting $a$ and $\mathbf{B}$ can be computed together in closed form, exactly as for the straight line.

## The point of variable projection

The full model is non-linear only through $\tau$ and $\alpha$. Variable projection (VarPro) exploits this structure:

1. For any candidate pair $(\tau, \alpha)$, the intercept and coefficients $(ct, cc, S2)$ are obtained analytically by least squares. They are never searched for.
2. The optimisation therefore reduces from a five-parameter nonlinear search to a two-parameter search over $(\tau, \alpha)$ alone.

This separation brings practical benefits. The search space collapses from five dimensions to two, so the fit is faster and far less prone to local minima. No starting guesses are required for the linear parameters, which removes a common source of fitting failure in clinical data. The two-dimensional $(\tau, \alpha)$ space is small enough to search exhaustively over a grid, giving a deterministic and reproducible fit.

# The design matrix

For $n$ observations $(t_i, y_i)$ and a fixed candidate pair $(\tau, \alpha)$, define the $n \times 3$ design matrix
$$
A(\tau, \alpha) =
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & e^{-t_1/\tau} & (t_1 - \alpha)H(t_1 - \alpha) \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
1 & e^{-t_n/\tau} & (t_n - \alpha)H(t_n - \alpha)
\end{pmatrix},
$$
whose columns are the constant, the cone basis function $f_1$, and the rod ramp $f_2$. The inner problem is then ordinary least squares,
$$
\hat{\theta}(\tau, \alpha) = \arg\min_{\theta} \lVert \mathbf{Y} - A(\tau,\alpha)\,\theta \rVert^2,
\qquad \theta = (ct,\ cc,\ S2)^{\top}.
$$

In R the matrix is one line; note that $(t-\alpha)H(t-\alpha)$ is simply `pmax(t - alpha, 0)`:

```{r design-matrix}
build_A <- function(t, tau, alpha) {
  cbind(1, exp(-t / tau), pmax(t - alpha, 0))
}
```

# The inner solve: normal equations and QR

The textbook solution of the inner problem is via the normal equations,
$$
\hat{\theta} = (A^{\top}A)^{-1} A^{\top} \mathbf{Y}.
$$
The implementation instead uses the QR decomposition $A = QR$, giving
$$
\hat{\theta} = R^{-1} Q^{\top} \mathbf{Y},
$$
computed by back-substitution without ever forming $A^{\top}A$.

```{r inner-solve}
solve_inner <- function(t, y, tau, alpha) {
  qrA <- qr(build_A(t, tau, alpha))
  list(theta = qr.coef(qrA, y),
       rss   = sum(qr.resid(qrA, y)^2))
}
```

The choice matters because forming $A^{\top}A$ squares the condition number, $\kappa(A^{\top}A) = \kappa(A)^2$, and our design matrix is ill-conditioned in exactly the regimes that occur in practice. When $\tau$ is large relative to the test window, the exponential column flattens towards an affine function of $t$; when $\alpha$ is small, the ramp column is close to an affine function of $t$ as well; together with the constant column the matrix approaches rank deficiency. The following makes the effect concrete:

```{r conditioning}
t_demo <- seq(0, 15, by = 1/3)
A_typical <- build_A(t_demo, tau = 1.2, alpha = 3.8)
A_ill     <- build_A(t_demo, tau = 200, alpha = 0.1)
c(kappa_typical    = kappa(A_typical),
  kappa_ill        = kappa(A_ill),
  kappa_normal_eqs = kappa(crossprod(A_ill)))
```

QR works at the condition number of $A$ itself; the normal equations work at its square, which in the ill-conditioned case above is of order $10^9$ and approaching the limit of double precision. Interior grid points are well conditioned; QR ensures the boundary of the grid is handled as accurately as the interior.

# Why it is called projection

The fitted values for a candidate pair are the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{Y}$ onto the column space of $A(\tau,\alpha)$. Writing $P_{A} = QQ^{\top}$ for the projector, the residual sum of squares that the outer search minimises is
$$
r(\tau, \alpha) = \lVert (I - P_{A})\,\mathbf{Y} \rVert^2,
$$
the squared length of the component of the data orthogonal to everything the linear parameters can explain. The linear parameters have been projected out of the problem, hence the name. The identity is easily verified numerically:

```{r projector}
set.seed(1)
y_demo <- rnorm(length(t_demo))
s  <- solve_inner(t_demo, y_demo, tau = 1.2, alpha = 3.8)
Q  <- qr.Q(qr(build_A(t_demo, tau = 1.2, alpha = 3.8)))
rss_projector <- sum(((diag(length(y_demo)) - Q %*% t(Q)) %*% y_demo)^2)
all.equal(rss_projector, s$rss)
```

# The outer search

## Grid and bounds

The grid over $(\tau, \alpha)$ is bounded by physiology and protocol, consistent with Section 6 of DISC-IP-003. Operational experience shows the cone time constant is usually below two minutes, so $\tau \in (0, 2]$ min. The range of $\alpha$ is contingent on the flash intensity of the test protocol; a fitted $\alpha$ beyond five minutes indicates a profound bleach rather than a physiological result, so $\alpha \in (0, 10]$ min, with the upper bound set here for illustrative purposes, the reported value acts as a validity check on the bleaching stage.

```{r grid-spec}
tau_grid   <- seq(0.05, 2.00, by = 0.05)   # 40 values
alpha_grid <- seq(0.50, 10.00, length.out=99)   # 99 values ~ 5.82 seconds
length(tau_grid) * length(alpha_grid)      # total closed-form solves
```

## The loop, cost, and tie-breaking

```{r outer-loop}
fit_varpro <- function(t, y, tau_grid, alpha_grid) {
  best <- list(rss = Inf)
  for (tau in tau_grid) for (alpha in alpha_grid) {
    s <- solve_inner(t, y, tau, alpha)
    if (s$rss < best$rss)
      best <- list(theta = s$theta, rss = s$rss, tau = tau, alpha = alpha)
  }
  best
}
```

The cost is exactly one $n \times 3$ QR decomposition per grid cell: fixed, data-independent, and known in advance. This is the appendix-level substantiation of the bounded-cost claim of DISC-IP-003. The strict inequality `s$rss < best$rss` is the tie-break rule: if two cells ever produce identical residuals, the first encountered in the fixed scan order (row-major over `tau_grid` then `alpha_grid`) is kept. The rule is stated so that the determinism claim, identical data yield identical parameters, holds without qualification.

# Numerical demonstration

We simulate a recovery curve with known parameters, sampled at three thresholds per minute over a fifteen-minute test, and fit it with the exhaustive grid at two noise levels: a clinically realistic threshold noise of 0.10 log units, and a low-noise condition of 0.02 log units.

```{r demonstration}
model <- function(t, p) p["ct"] + p["cc"] * exp(-t / p["tau"]) +
  p["S2"] * pmax(t - p["alpha"], 0)

truth <- c(ct = 1.0, cc = 2.0, tau = 1.2, alpha = 3.8, S2 = -0.25)
t_obs <- seq(0, 15, by = 1/3)

set.seed(1)
y_noisy <- model(t_obs, truth) + rnorm(length(t_obs), sd = 0.10)
y_clean <- model(t_obs, truth) + rnorm(length(t_obs), sd = 0.02)

elapsed_noisy <- system.time(
  fit_noisy <- fit_varpro(t_obs, y_noisy, tau_grid, alpha_grid)
)["elapsed"]

elapsed_clear <- system.time(
  fit_clean <- fit_varpro(t_obs, y_clean, tau_grid, alpha_grid)
)["elapsed"]

data.frame(
  parameter        = names(truth),
  truth            = as.numeric(truth),
  fit_sd_0.10      = round(c(fit_noisy$theta[1:2], fit_noisy$tau,
                             fit_noisy$alpha, fit_noisy$theta[3]), 3),
  fit_sd_0.02      = round(c(fit_clean$theta[1:2], fit_clean$tau,
                             fit_clean$alpha, fit_clean$theta[3]), 3),
  row.names = NULL
)
elapsed_noisy
elapsed_clear
t_del <- elapsed_noisy - elapsed_clear
t_del
```

Two observations. First, the full grid of `r length(tau_grid) * length(alpha_grid)` closed-form solves completes in a fraction of a second on a laptop in interpreted R; a compiled implementation on device hardware is faster still, and the cost is fixed regardless of the data. Second, the parameters differ in how sharply the data constrain them. The linear parameters and $\tau$ are recovered closely even at clinical noise. The break time $\alpha$ carries the widest uncertainty of the five: the ramp contributes almost nothing to the fit in the neighbourhood of the break, so observations there carry little information about its exact position. At clinical noise the grid recovery is within a few tenths of a minute; at low noise it converges to the truth. This is a property of the estimation problem, not of the method; any fitting procedure faces it, and the exhaustive grid at least guarantees that the reported $\alpha$ is the best available over the whole physiological range.

```{r fit-plot, fig.height=4.5, fig.width=7}
par(las=1, bty = 'n')
plot(t_obs, y_noisy, pch = 16, cex = 0.7, col = "grey40",
     xlab = "Time in the dark (min)", ylab = "Threshold (log units)")
t_fine <- seq(0, 15, by = 0.02)
fitted_p <- c(ct = unname(fit_noisy$theta[1]), cc = unname(fit_noisy$theta[2]),
              tau = fit_noisy$tau, alpha = fit_noisy$alpha,
              S2 = unname(fit_noisy$theta[3]))
lines(t_fine, model(t_fine, truth),    lty = 2)
lines(t_fine, model(t_fine, fitted_p), lwd = 2)
legend("topright", c("truth", "fitted"), lty = c(2, 1), lwd = c(1, 2), bty = "n")
```

# Edge cases

**No break within the test window.** If a candidate $\alpha$ meets or exceeds the largest observation time, the ramp column of $A$ is identically zero and the matrix is rank deficient. R's rank-revealing QR handles this gracefully, returning `NA` for the unidentifiable coefficient while still fitting the remaining two columns:

```{r rank-deficient}
solve_inner(t_obs, y_noisy, tau = 1.2, alpha = 20)$theta
```

In the implementation this case is excluded by construction: the grid's upper bound of ten minutes sits well inside the test window, so every candidate design matrix has full rank. Should a participant genuinely show no break within the window, the best fit lands at the boundary of the grid and is reported as such, flagging the test rather than silently extrapolating.

**Thresholds censored at the instrument floor.** Early in recovery, thresholds can sit at the maximum stimulus intensity the instrument can present. Such observations are ceiling-censored: the true threshold is at or above the recorded value. Treating them as exact biases $cc$ and $\tau$ downwards. The implementation's treatment of censored points, exclusion from the fit or a censored-likelihood weighting, will be stated here once finalised for the Mk3.

**Ties.** Covered above: strict inequality with a fixed scan order makes the selection deterministic even in the measure-zero event of equal residuals.

# Determinism and cross-platform reproducibility

<!-- Replacement for the "Determinism across platforms" section of
     DISC-IP-003-appendix-A.Rmd. Revised 22 August 2026 against the
     complete macOS/RISC-V comparison (both platforms ran the full
     experiment; the earlier truncated run is superseded). Numbers below
     are final. -->

The method is deterministic by construction: a fixed grid, a closed-form
solve at each cell, and a stated tie-break. On a single platform,
identical data yield bit-identical parameters. Across platforms, exact
agreement additionally depends on the floating-point summation order
inside the linear algebra library, which differs between builds. This
section reports a direct measurement of that agreement.

## Design of the comparison

The complete validation experiment was executed on two machines under the
same repository commit, verified identical by `git diff`, with the
pseudo-random number generator version pinned so that both platforms
simulate identical data:

| | Development platform | Independent platform |
|---|---|---|
| Architecture | arm64 (Apple silicon) | riscv64 (UltraRISC UR-DP1000) |
| Operating system | macOS | Ubuntu |
| R version | 4.5.2 | 4.3.3 |
| BLAS | Accelerate / vecLib | reference BLAS |

The two builds therefore differ in instruction set architecture, operating
system, R version, and linear algebra implementation: close to a worst
case for exact agreement.

**Inputs are bit-identical.** Under the pinned generator, the same seed
produces the same pseudo-random draws on both machines, verified to the
last bit by comparing the exact hexadecimal representation of the values
(`sprintf("%a", ...)`). Every simulated recovery curve is therefore
identical on the two platforms, and any difference in the fitted
parameters is attributable to the fitting arithmetic alone.

The comparison covers 191,996 replications: the four cone-time-constant
sets in full, on both platforms.

## Results

Fits at the lower bound of the $\tau$ grid are excluded from the
parameter comparison and reported separately: there the cone exponential
collapses over the sampled interval and the cone coefficient is
unidentified, taking values of order $10^{13}$ on both platforms. These
accounted for 15,271 replications, 8.0% of the total. Both platforms
reached the same degenerate solution in every such case, agreeing to
seven significant figures.

Over the remaining 176,725 identified fits:

| Cone time constant $\tau$ | 0.6 | 1.2 | 1.8 | 2.4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Identified fits compared | 44,165 | 43,995 | 43,913 | 44,652 |
| Residual sum of squares bit-identical | 76.5% | 76.0% | 75.7% | 75.8% |
| RSS difference, 99th percentile | $1.0\times10^{-14}$ | $1.0\times10^{-14}$ | $1.0\times10^{-14}$ | $1.0\times10^{-14}$ |
| RSS difference, 99.9th percentile | $1.1\times10^{-14}$ | $1.1\times10^{-14}$ | $1.1\times10^{-14}$ | $1.7\times10^{-6}$ |
| Largest RSS difference | $2.2\times10^{-4}$ | $1.2\times10^{-5}$ | $7.1\times10^{-4}$ | $8.0\times10^{-4}$ |
| Break times differing by more than $10^{-6}$ min | 2 | 1 | 4 | 60 |
| Boundary classification disagreements | 0 | 0 | 1 | 0 |

Roughly three quarters of all fits are bit-identical across the two
architectures, and the residual sum of squares agrees to
$1\times10^{-14}$ in 99% of cases in every cone regime. Classification of
the fitted slope as interior or at a bound agreed in 191,995 of 191,996
comparisons: a single disagreement in the whole experiment.

## The source and size of the exceptions

Where the two platforms differ, the difference arises at one specific
point in the pipeline, and not in the exhaustive search. In every case
examined the two platforms selected the same winning grid cell, with
identical grid parameters and grid residual. The divergence occurs in the
subsequent continuous refinement, at the test that decides whether the
refined solution is accepted:

$$\text{accept if } \mathrm{RSS}_{\text{refined}} < \mathrm{RSS}_{\text{grid}}.$$

When the refinement improves the residual only at the level of
floating-point rounding, this strict comparison can fall either way, and
the two platforms then report the two endpoints of a step that made no
material difference to the fit. Across the four sets this occurred in 1,
1, 1, and 53 replications respectively.

**The exceptions concentrate in the ill-conditioned regime.** Both the
count of accept-test disagreements (1, 1, 1, 53) and the count of
materially differing break times (2, 1, 4, 60) rise by more than an order
of magnitude at the longest cone time constant, while the other three
regimes remain at one to four. This is expected from the geometry of the
problem. When $\tau$ is long relative to the test window, the cone
exponential approaches an affine function of time and the error surface
develops a ridge along which the parameters trade off; refinement gains
along such a ridge are small, so the accept test is more often decided by
rounding. The same regime is the only one in which the 99.9th percentile
of the residual difference leaves rounding territory at all.

The practical size of the exceptions is negligible. The largest
disagreement in break time anywhere in the comparison was 0.43 minutes,
in a replication with *no true rod phase* where both platforms returned a
fitted slope of about $-0.001$; the remaining worst cases differ by 0.05
to 0.38 minutes, that is, three to twenty-three seconds, against
confidence intervals for the break time that are 1.5 to 4 minutes wide.
In these replications the residual sums of squares agree to four
significant figures or better: the two platforms have found fits of
indistinguishable quality and differ only in which of two near-equivalent
parameter sets they report.

## Statement

Identical inputs, verified bit-identical across architectures, produce
fits that are bit-identical in roughly three quarters of cases and agree
to $1\times10^{-14}$ in residual sum of squares in 99% of cases, despite
differences in instruction set, operating system, R version, and linear
algebra implementation. The exhaustive profiled search itself agreed
exactly in every case examined, and the classification of the fitted
slope agreed in all but one of 191,996 comparisons. The rare exceptions
arise from the accept test of the optional refinement stage when its
improvement is at the level of rounding, concentrate in the
ill-conditioned cone regime, and are immaterial by any clinical or
statistical measure.

If bit-level cross-platform identity were ever required, two routes are
available: omitting the refinement stage, which the validation experiment
shows contributes a median residual improvement of well under one per cent
and parameter shifts of a fraction of a grid step; or replacing the
accept test with a tolerance, so that a refinement is accepted only when
it improves the residual by more than a stated margin.
